Heure Universelle & Louis Cottier
Louis Cottier (1894-1966) developed his ingenious World Time, or ‘Heure Universelle’, mechanism in 1931. Allowing the simultaneous reading of the time across multiple locations around the world, the system would become one of the most celebrated and recognisable complications of 20th-century watchmaking. Cottier’s invention was subsequently adopted by several of Switzerland’s most prestigious manufactures, including Patek Philippe for references 605, 1415 and 2523, Vacheron Constantin for reference 3372, as well as Agassiz and Rolex for reference 4262.

Cottier continued to refine his invention throughout his career. In 1953, he developed a mechanism allowing the city disc to be adjusted by means of a secondary crown. Further development resulted in a system patented by Patek Philippe in 1958, permitting the hour hand to be adjusted independently without interrupting the continuous progression of the minute hand.

Ingenious in its construction yet remarkably intuitive in use, Cottier’s Heure Universelle remains one of the most elegant solutions ever devised for displaying world time. Reference 605 occupies an important position within this history, translating the complication into the classical proportions of a Patek Philippe pocket watch and representing one of the earliest and rarest expressions of the manufacture’s enduring association with Louis Cottier.

Today, stainless steel is the material of choice for many of the world's most coveted wristwatches, yet this was far from the case throughout much of the twentieth century. While steel had long been used for balance springs and technical components, its sensitivity to temperature made it unsuitable for precision timekeeping. During the 1930s, manufacturers such as Omega and Longines increasingly adopted stainless steel for robust military and chronograph wristwatches, while Patek Philippe was among the first high watchmaking manufactures to embrace the material for serial production with the waterproof Calatrava reference 565, broadening its appeal in the years following the Great Depression.

The true turning point, however, came in 1972 with the introduction of Audemars Piguet's Royal Oak. Designed by Gérald Genta, it became the first serially produced luxury sports watch in stainless steel, forever changing collectors' perception of the material. Its success inspired an entirely new category of high-end sports timepieces, including Patek Philippe's Nautilus, likewise designed by Genta only a few years later.

Against this historical backdrop, the decision by A. Lange & Söhne to produce a stainless steel Lange 1 was nothing short of extraordinary. Günter Blümlein, the visionary behind the manufacture's revival, had publicly maintained that steel had no place within the brand's philosophy, famously declaring that if the market demanded steel, 'it has to get steel, but not at A. Research indicates that less than thirty stainless steel Lange 1 examples were delivered to retailers worldwide. Pisa Orologeria received twenty watches, seventeen with silver dials and three with black dials, while New York retailer Cellini Jewelers ordered eight but ultimately received only four. Lange & Söhne has confirmed that the original silver dial was later replaced at the manufacture with the present blue dial. To the best of our knowledge, only two stainless steel Lange 1 examples fitted with a blue dial are currently known.

The origins of the Vagabondage collection can be traced back to 1997, when François-Paul Journe created a unique wristwatch for a close friend known as the Carpe Diem. Housed in a round yellow gold case, it featured an automatic movement and an unconventional display combining wandering hours with a central exposed balance wheel. Journe later revisited the concept, developing a manually wound wristwatch with a similar display housed in a tortue-shaped case. Although a prototype was completed, the project was ultimately set aside as the manufacture's attention turned to other developments.

The design resurfaced in 2003 when Antiquorum invited François-Paul Journe to create a unique timepiece for its 30th Anniversary charity auction benefiting the ICM Foundation. Faced with an ambitious six-month deadline, Journe chose to reinterpret the sleeping Vagabondage prototype rather than develop an entirely new concept. The result was three unique watches, executed in yellow, pink, and white gold respectively, each fitted with a brass movement. In keeping with the purity of the design, the dial deliberately omitted the F.P. Journe signature. Following the overwhelming success of the auction and strong demand from collectors, Journe agreed to place the model into regular production, albeit in extremely limited numbers due to its distinctive aesthetic within the manufacture's catalogue.

The first production series, the Vagabondage I, was introduced in 2004 in a limited edition of 69 platinum examples, complemented by ten additional pieces set with baguette-cut diamonds. The Vagabondage II followed in 2010, with production expanded to include both platinum and 68 pink gold examples. In recognition of the loyalty of existing collectors, owners of a Vagabondage I were given priority to acquire a Vagabondage II bearing the same individual number, a tradition that continued with the release of the Vagabondage III in 2017.

Christie’s is thrilled to present for the first time at auction this extraordinary yellow gold Nautilus reference 3700⁄1, made for His Majesty Sultan Qaboos bin Said al Said of Oman in 1978. Among the rarest and most elusive of all vintage gold Nautilus watches, the present example is, to the best of our knowledge, fresh to the market and was previously unknown to scholars and collectors.

Until the discovery of the present watch, only five examples of the yellow gold reference 3700 with ‘Khanjar’ dial were publicly known. This remarkable watch, now the sixth known example, therefore represents one of the most important additions to the scholarship surrounding the legendary reference in recent years. Adding further to its significance, it has survived in superb original condition. The dial remains completely untouched and is beginning to display the first signs of tropicalisation at its centre, notably between 3 and 4 o’clock, while the gold-coloured ‘Khanjar’ emblem of the Sultanate of Oman is beautifully printed above 6 o’clock. The last three digits of the case number, ‘366’, are correctly engraved to the underside of the bezel.

Of exceptional importance, the present timepiece comes directly from its original owner, who worked in close proximity to His Majesty Sultan Qaboos bin Said al Said. Its provenance is accompanied by the recipient’s own remarkable account of his relationship with the Sultan and of the circumstances that ultimately led to him receiving the present watch.

As a young man, during his first meeting with Sultan Qaboos at the Palace, the future owner was asked the time. Not wearing a watch, he was unable to answer. The Sultan consequently gave him a wristwatch, a gesture whose deeper significance the recipient admits he did not fully appreciate at the time. On subsequent occasions, the Sultan noticed that he was again without the watch. When told that it had first been forgotten and later lost, His Majesty expressed his disappointment, impressing upon the young man the importance of respecting time and the responsibility associated with something that had been entrusted to him.

The lesson continued. After seeing him wearing an inexpensive replacement watch, Sultan Qaboos reminded him of the significance of the watch he had originally been given and subsequently instructed him not to wear a watch while on duty. Yet he continued to ask him the time. Faced with the challenge of answering without consulting a timepiece, the young man gradually learned to observe the passage of the hours and minutes and to estimate the time with increasing accuracy. Eventually, when his answers became consistently close, the Sultan would tell him that his affairs were ‘in good order’.

Only with time did the recipient come to understand that these exchanges were never simply about knowing the hour. As he recalls, they were lessons in ‘discipline, attentiveness, responsibility, and respect for the value of every moment’. The present Patek Philippe Nautilus was subsequently bestowed upon him by Sultan Qaboos and became far more than a precious object: it embodied the trust placed in him and the lessons learned during his years of service. Preserved by its recipient ever since, the watch remains for him a lasting reminder of the man who taught him to value time.

With movement no. 1’305’233 and case no. 537’366, the present watch is the latest-numbered example of the six so far discovered. Significantly, the known timepieces bear movement and case numbers in extremely close proximity, in some instances separated by only two or three numbers. Further strengthening the connection between these examples, another timepiece shares the exact same date of sale as the present timepiece, 23 November 1978. This remarkable proximity in numbering and identical date of sale strongly indicates that the watches formed part of a specially designated order produced for His Majesty Sultan Qaboos bin Said al Said.

Faithful to Vianney Halter's unmistakable design language, the present Trio Grande Date draws heavily on the nautical inspirations that define many of his creations. The bezel evokes the appearance of a ship's porthole, while the riveted crown reinforces the industrial, marine-inspired aesthetic. In keeping with Halter's philosophy of mechanical transparency, the watch is fitted with his patented mysterious mass winding system. Unlike a conventional automatic rotor, the oscillating weight is concealed beneath a peripheral ring, creating the illusion of a manually wound movement while allowing an uninterrupted view of the calibre through the sapphire crystal caseback. Reportedly, only 10 examples in white gold were ever produced, making the present timepiece one of the rarest creations from Vianney Halter's already highly exclusive production.

The origins of the Trio date back to the late 1990s, when Halter conceived a highly original wristwatch featuring three separate portholes, hence the name, for the hours and minutes, running seconds, and date. Although this first iteration remained at the prototype stage, the concept laid the foundations for the present model. In the early 2000s, Halter revisited the design, introducing a large double-disc date that required the addition of a fourth porthole while significantly enhancing the watch's practicality.

Far more than a simple enlargement of the date display, Halter completely re-engineered the movement to incorporate an ingenious gear system allowing rapid date adjustment directly via the crown. The time-setting and date-setting mechanisms operate entirely independently, ensuring that adjusting one function has no effect on the other. With the crown in its neutral position, the date advances automatically at midnight, while a day/night indicator on the main dial prevents any accidental date change at noon. This thoughtful mechanical solution perfectly illustrates Vianney Halter's ability to combine technical innovation with intuitive functionality, reinforcing the Trio Grande Date as one of the most original creations of contemporary independent watchmaking.

Calibre 28 SC
Providing a power reserve of approximately 65 hours, the calibre 28 SC marked the first Voutilainen movement to incorporate central seconds. Its architecture is distinguished by rose gold wheels and a large 13.60 mm free-sprung balance fitted with a Breguet/Grossmann balance spring and rose gold inertia blocks.

At the heart of the movement is Voutilainen’s direct-impulse escapement, inspired by Breguet’s échappement naturel. Employing two escape wheels that deliver direct impulses to the balance, the system reduces the energy losses associated with a conventional Swiss lever escapement, contributing to greater efficiency and stability. Voutilainen was the first contemporary watchmaker to employ a two-wheel direct-impulse escapement in this particular configuration.

Kari Voutilainen
Born in Finland in 1962, Kari Voutilainen trained at the renowned watchmaking school of Tapiola before continuing his studies at WOSTEP in Neuchâtel in 1990. He subsequently spent nine years working at the atelier of Parmigiani, followed by several years teaching watchmaking at WOSTEP.

In 2002, Voutilainen established himself as an independent watchmaker in Môtiers, Switzerland. His dedication to traditional methods, exceptional hand-finishing and innovative movement construction has since established him as one of the leading figures of contemporary independent watchmaking.

The present timepiece is not only a great rarity from Cartier’s London workshops, but has also survived in remarkable condition. A masterclass in simplicity of design, it nevertheless achieves a dramatic aesthetic that was completely avant-garde for a wristwatch in 1970. The elongated rectangular case, with its integral fittings for the two straps, is defined by broad, tapered sides that give the watch both substance and visual solidity, further accentuated by the oversized beaded cabochon-set crown. The painted dial, signed ‘Cartier London’, is a beautifully original creation, characterised by ‘exploding’ hour indexes and large, bold Roman half-hour numerals. The watch is powered by a Jaeger-LeCoultre movement, numbered 1’949’458, entirely correct for a London-made Cartier wristwatch of this period. The association between Louis Cartier and Edmond Jaeger began in the early years of the 20th century and, even after Jaeger’s death, the collaboration between Cartier and LeCoultre continued for decades. Jean-Jacques Cartier was still using LeCoultre movements for his creations throughout the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, regarding them as among the finest movements available.

Cartier’s celebrated motto, ‘Never Copy, Only Create’, has particular resonance when considering the extraordinarily imaginative wristwatches that emerged from the London workshops during the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s. Each was handmade and produced in extremely small numbers, making them exceptionally difficult to obtain even at the time. Instantly recognisable and highly exclusive, Cartier London watches have today become stellar rarities among vintage wristwatches and some of the most aspirational creations for collectors of vintage Cartier.

London during the 1960s and 1970s was a centre of extraordinary cultural and creative energy, and Jean-Jacques Cartier, who had instigated the production of Cartier watches in London, sought to create wristwatches that truly reflected the spirit of the period. The designs that emerged from the workshops, including the legendary Crash and the present ‘Twin Strap’, were not merely avant-garde but deliberately provocative. Their extraordinary, head-turning forms stood in complete contrast to the conservative round and rectangular wristwatches that dominated contemporary watchmaking, making the present example a remarkable testament to one of the most creative periods in Cartier’s history.

The rarest of all perpetual calendar wristwatches produced in series by Patek Philippe, this superb reference 2438⁄1 exudes the distinctive and almost magical vintage appeal of the company’s mid-century complicated wristwatches. With a total production believed to comprise only around 65 pieces in yellow and pink gold, it is by far the rarest serially produced perpetual calendar model by the manufacture. More significantly, reference 2438⁄1 was the world’s first serially produced waterproof perpetual calendar wristwatch, an extraordinarily forward-thinking proposition for the early 1950s. Indeed, the market was perhaps not yet ready for such a timepiece: following its discontinuation, no comparable serially produced water-resistant perpetual calendar wristwatch would appear for decades.

Launched in 1951 alongside its non-waterproof sibling, reference 2497, reference 2438⁄1 remained in production until 1963. Adding another important chapter to their history, the two references were Patek Philippe’s first serially produced perpetual calendar wristwatches with centre seconds. Following their discontinuation, the manufacture would not revisit this combination until 1993 with the introduction of reference 5050.

Aesthetically, reference 2438⁄1 is a masterpiece of mid-century horological design, characterised by beautifully balanced symmetry, spectacular curves and generous proportions. Its architecture bears a close resemblance to the legendary reference 2499, introduced at approximately the same time and, with few exceptions, made by the same celebrated casemaker, Wenger. The two references consequently share much of the same design language, the principal visual differences being the absence of the chronograph complication on reference 2438⁄1 and the relocation of the running seconds from 9 o’clock to the centre.

It is believed that only approximately 50 examples of reference 2438⁄1 were made in yellow gold, of which around 30 are publicly known today. The reference is generally divided into two series. First-series watches feature applied Arabic numerals and feuille hands, while second-series examples are distinguished by applied baton numerals and dauphine hands. The second series can be further separated into two dial variations: Mark I, with five-faceted hour markers, as seen on the present timepiece, and Mark II, with rectangular four-faceted hour markers.

Made by Stern Frères on a solid gold base, the dial is finished with an elegant opaline-matte surface. The English-language calendar discs are fashioned from silvered gold, while the moon-phase disc is handmade in gold with champlevé blue enamel applied by a master enameller.

The addition of centre seconds could not simply be achieved by adapting the calibre 13’’-130 employed in reference 2499. Patek Philippe therefore turned to the calibre 27SC, regarded as one of the finest centre-seconds movements of its era, and developed a perpetual calendar module specifically for it. The John Schaeffer collection
The introduction of the John Schaeffer collection coincided with Audemars Piguet’s important revival of complicated wristwatches, particularly minute repeaters and other striking mechanisms for which the manufacture had already become renowned during the early decades of the 20th century. Its distinctive cushion-shaped architecture provided an ideal framework for a series of highly complicated watches inspired by some of Audemars Piguet’s earliest masterpieces.

The collection took its design directly from an important minute-repeating wristwatch made for John Wallace Schaeffer, vice president of the Allied Chemical Corporation in Morristown, New Jersey, in 1927. Its distinctive ‘coussin tortue’ case was complemented by a highly personal dial on which the conventional hour numerals were replaced by the twelve letters spelling ‘JOHN SCHAEFFER’.

Following its acquisition by the Audemars Piguet Museum, Schaeffer’s original watch was publicly exhibited in 1992. Its enthusiastic reception inspired the manufacture to revisit the historic design and create an entirely new collection bearing the John Schaeffer name. The resulting watches combined the characteristic cushion-shaped case with some of Audemars Piguet’s most sophisticated complications, creating a direct link between the manufacture’s historic complicated wristwatches and its modern production.

The Cartier Crash
The origins of the Cartier Crash were for many years surrounded by myths and speculation, encouraged in part by the absence of widely available documentation. Greater clarity emerged with Francesca Cartier Brickell’s 2019 book 'The Cartiers: The Untold Story of the Family Behind the Jewellery Empire', based on extensive research into the Cartier family history.

Created in the vibrant cultural atmosphere of 1960s London, the Crash was conceived by Jean-Jacques Cartier in collaboration with designer Rupert Emmerson. Jean-Jacques sought to create a wristwatch that reflected the energy and creativity of the period, and after considerable experimentation, the pair arrived at a radically unconventional design far removed from the geometric forms and straight lines traditionally associated with watches such as the Tank.

With its fluid, asymmetrical case and specially conceived distorted dial, the Crash is immediately recognisable. More than half a century after its creation, its unconventional proportions remain remarkably contemporary, demonstrating the originality of Cartier London’s approach to watch design during one of the Maison’s most creative periods.

Patek Philippe pocket watches featuring a split-seconds chronograph without any additional complication are rare, and the exceptional quality of the present timepiece is evident throughout its construction, including refined details such as the concealed case hinge.

Patek Philippe began producing split-seconds chronographs in the late 1870s, followed in 1902 by the granting of the company’s own patent for a split-seconds chronograph mechanism. The complication subsequently became one of the manufacture’s specialities, with a significant proportion of production destined for export, most probably including the present timepiece. The interior of its caseback bears the French ‘owl’ importation gold mark, while the dial is signed ‘FAB. SUISSE’ below 6 o’clock, a designation used on watches intended for export to France.

Even in a world where the wristwatch now reigns supreme, complicated pocket watches, particularly those made by Patek Philippe, remain a source of enduring fascination. The pursuit of ever greater timekeeping accuracy and technical complexity, supported by extraordinary mathematical and mechanical ingenuity, played a fundamental role in establishing and cementing Patek Philippe’s reputation as one of the world’s greatest watchmaking houses from the late 19th century to the present day.

The split-seconds chronograph is considered one of the classic complications of traditional watchmaking, requiring the coordination of two chronograph seconds hands to allow the timing of simultaneous or intermediate events. Patek Philippe’s executions of this sophisticated mechanism during the early 20th century are regarded as among the finest ever made and remain true marvels of micromechanics from the period.

Then as now, Patek Philippe watches were highly coveted trophies, their ownership conveying an appreciation of exceptional craftsmanship, refinement and technical sophistication. Combining rarity, superb construction, and the exceptional survival of its original Certificate of Origin, the present split-seconds chronograph pocket watch is a particularly compelling example of the manufacture’s extraordinary mastery of complicated watchmaking.

 Reference 1518
 Introduced in 1941, reference 1518 holds an extraordinary place in horological history as the world's first serially produced perpetual calendar chronograph wristwatch. Together with its companion reference 1526, it also established Patek Philippe as the first manufacture to produce perpetual calendar wristwatches in series. From its introduction, the 1518 became one of the manufacture's most prestigious and desirable complicated wristwatches.

 At its heart is the celebrated calibre 13''' Q (13-130 Q), based on a Valjoux ébauche extensively modified and finished by Patek Philippe, with the perpetual calendar mechanism adapted by the workshops of Victorin Piguet. This movement architecture would form the mechanical foundation of Patek Philippe's perpetual calendar chronographs, including its successor reference 2499, for decades.

 The gold cases of reference 1518 were manufactured by Emile Vichet and evolved subtly throughout production. Earlier examples featured flatter cases with chronograph pushers positioned around the middle of the caseband, while later watches received more downward-curving lugs and lower-set pushers. From around 1949, larger crowns were also introduced.

 Demand for reference 1518 consistently exceeded its extremely limited production, with examples generally reserved by Patek Philippe retailers for their most important clients. According to research, only 281 examples were produced between 1941 and 1954, the great majority in yellow gold. It was subsequently succeeded by the equally legendary reference 2499, which retained the perpetual calendar chronograph architecture while introducing a larger case and distinctive fluted lugs.

With its charming silvered dial, the present F.P. Journe Tourbillon Souverain belongs to the highly coveted Reference T series and represents a particularly desirable third-generation example. The accompanying Certificate of Authenticity confirms that the watch was originally delivered in Switzerland in 2001, while its individual number, 125/01T, identifies it as the 125th example produced. Offered by the family of the original owner and as an early brass-movement Tourbillon Souverain from the formative years of the manufacture, the present timepiece occupies an important position in the history of F.P. Journe.

Introduced at Baselworld in 1999, the Tourbillon Souverain Reference T holds a special place in François-Paul Journe's career as his first series-produced wristwatch, following the celebrated group of 20 Souscription pieces. More significantly, it was the first wristwatch to incorporate a remontoir d'égalité, or constant-force mechanism. By regulating the energy transmitted from the mainspring to the escapement, the remontoir provides the tourbillon with a more consistent supply of torque, thereby improving chronometric stability throughout the watch's approximately 42-hour power reserve. The combination of these two mechanisms perfectly encapsulates Journe's philosophy: creating thoroughly contemporary and technically ambitious wristwatches firmly rooted in the traditions of classical horology.

Until the introduction of the Reference TN, or Tourbillon Nouveau, in April 2004, the Tourbillon Souverain was powered by the rhodium-plated brass calibre 1498. From 2004 onwards, F.P. Journe famously transitioned to movements constructed in 18k pink gold, with the new calibre 1403. Early brass-movement watches such as the present example therefore represent a distinct and historically significant chapter in the development of the manufacture and have become particularly prized by collectors.

Within the Reference T series, four distinct dial generations have been identified:

First generation
Souscription series: limited to just 20 pieces, sold to collectors who prepaid prior to completion. These watches are numbered 1⁄20 to 20⁄20 on both dial and case, with dials signed only 'Invenit et Fecit / F.P. Journe'. The remontoire cock is rounded.

Second generation
The first true Reference T production watches. Dials are signed 'Invenit et Fecit / F.P. Journe' and 'Remontoir d’Égalité'. As with the Souscription series, the remontoire cock remains rounded.

Third generation
Characterised by enlarged power reserve numerals, now almost matching the size of the minute numerals, and a flat remontoire cock, such as on the present timepiece.

Fourth generation
Distinguished by smaller dial screws, marking the final evolution of the Reference T dial design.

Combining an early 2001 production date, the coveted brass calibre 1498, third-generation characteristics, and individual number 125/01T, the present Tourbillon Souverain is an exceptional representative of F.P. Journe's formative period. Both technically groundbreaking and historically significant, it stands as one of the defining creations upon which the reputation of the modern manufacture was built.

Audemars Piguet has created some of the finest openworked wristwatches throughout its history, yet the combination of this traditional craft with the unmistakable architecture of the Royal Oak remains particularly striking. Beyond its visual impact, however, the present timepiece showcases one of the manufacture’s most ingenious contemporary technical developments: the Double Balance Wheel mechanism.

In a conventional mechanical watch, a single balance wheel and hairspring regulate the movement. When the watch changes position, gravity can influence the hairspring and consequently affect its precision. Audemars Piguet addressed this challenge with the introduction of the Double Balance Wheel Openworked, employing two balance wheels and two hairsprings assembled on the same axis. By increasing the stability of the regulating organ, this innovative construction improves precision while providing a spectacular focal point within the openworked movement.

The present timepiece is further distinguished by its ‘frosted’ finish, an aesthetic first introduced to the Royal Oak through Audemars Piguet’s collaboration with Florentine jewelry designer Carolina Bucci in 2016. Inspired by an ancient Florentine jewelry technique, the surface is repeatedly struck with a diamond-tipped tool, creating innumerable microscopic indentations that catch and reflect the light. The resulting granular texture gives the metal a remarkable sparkling appearance reminiscent of a surface set with tiny diamonds, while preserving the characteristic geometry of the Royal Oak.

Housed within a contemporary 37 mm. case, the openworked calibre 3132 provides an exceptional view of the mechanism from both sides of the watch. Its intricately skeletonised bridges are given a dark ruthenium treatment, creating a distinctive gunmetal appearance that contrasts dramatically with the balance bridge and further draws attention to the two superimposed balance wheels.

Introduced in 2010, reference 5950A immediately established itself as one of Patek Philippe’s most technically impressive and unconventional modern chronographs. Combining an exceptionally sophisticated split-seconds mechanism with a stainless steel Art Deco-inspired case, the reference deliberately departs from the traditional convention of housing the manufacture’s most complicated wristwatches exclusively in precious metals.

The cushion-shaped case draws its inspiration from Patek Philippe split-seconds chronographs of the 1920s and 1930s. Its period character is further enhanced by the silvery dial with blackened white gold Breguet numerals, an outer railway track with fifth-of-a-second divisions and two horizontally positioned subsidiary dials decorated with circular guilloché. Fine black-lacquered engraved motifs embellish each of the four corners of the dial, a decorative detail echoed on the movement and testament to Patek Philippe’s meticulous attention to detail.

At the heart of reference 5950A is the manually wound calibre CHR 27-525 PS, originally introduced in 2005 with reference 5959. Developed entirely in-house, it was Patek Philippe’s first proprietary chronograph movement and, at the time of its introduction, the thinnest manually wound column-wheel split-seconds chronograph movement ever created. Its remarkably slender construction allows the reference 5950A to maintain an exceptionally elegant profile despite the complexity of its rattrapante mechanism.

Each CHR 27-525 PS calibre was individually produced and finished within Patek Philippe’s haute horlogerie ateliers. Its components were individually filed, bevelled, polished and adjusted before undergoing an initial assembly and testing process known as ‘repassage en blanc’. The movement was then completely dismantled, cleaned, reassembled, lubricated and finally regulated. Visible through the sapphire crystal caseback, its exceptional finishing is further distinguished by the Patek Philippe Seal.

The significance of reference 5950A is heightened by its stainless steel construction. The ‘A’ suffix stands for ‘acier’, French for steel, and the model represented Patek Philippe’s first split-seconds chronograph wristwatch housed in this metal. Bringing together an extraordinarily sophisticated movement, a historically inspired design and the unusual use of stainless steel, reference 5950A occupies a particularly distinctive position among Patek Philippe’s modern complicated wristwatches.

The model quickly gained recognition among researchers, notably those working at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) in Geneva. At the time of its introduction, the Milgauss represented a remarkable technical achievement, maintaining its precision when exposed to magnetic fields of 1,000 oersted, while tests demonstrated reliable performance even at significantly higher levels.

This exceptional resistance was achieved through the use of a soft iron inner case forming a Faraday cage, effectively shielding the movement from magnetic interference. Named after the English scientist Michael Faraday, whose pioneering experiments demonstrated the protective effect of conductive enclosures against electrical fields, the principle remains one of the most effective solutions for protecting mechanical movements from magnetism. Early reference 6541 models were further equipped with distinctive honeycomb dials, formed from two crossed aluminium layers to provide additional protection against electromagnetic radiation, such as the present timepiece.

This phenomenon later fascinated great horologists including Abraham-Louis Breguet and Antide Janvier, both of whom experimented with resonance in portable timekeepers. Although Breguet produced only three resonance pocket watches in the early nineteenth century, it was François-Paul Journe who ultimately succeeded in miniaturising this remarkable principle into a wristwatch. Within the Chronomètre à Résonance, two balances progressively synchronise with one another, significantly improving chronometric stability by reducing the effects of external disturbances. The present Upside Down is a remarkable expression of Ludovic Ballouard’s imaginative approach to mechanical watchmaking. Its ingenious display features eleven hour numerals appearing ‘upside down’, while at the turn of each hour the corresponding numeral rotates 180 degrees to reveal itself ‘right side up’. Combining mechanical ingenuity with a remarkably balanced design, the Upside Down has become one of the defining creations of contemporary independent watchmaking.

The present example is rendered particularly exceptional by its platinum case and spectacular blue-green dial crafted from Henbury meteorite. The material’s naturally occurring crystalline structure creates an intricate surface whose appearance shifts with the light, ensuring that no two dials can ever be precisely alike. Produced in an extremely limited edition of only seven pieces, the present watch is numbered 5 of 7.

After many years working as a watchmaker, Ballouard decided in May 2009 to pursue his ambition of creating his own unconventional complications. The Upside Down, unveiled later that same year, became his first creation under his own name. Beyond its technical originality, its unusual display carries a philosophical dimension: the elapsed hours are turned upside down and the hours yet to come remain similarly inverted, leaving only the present hour correctly oriented. In Ballouard’s conception, the mechanism serves as a reminder that the past cannot be changed and the future remains unknown, placing emphasis firmly on the present moment.

Henbury meteorite
The Henbury meteorite is believed to originate from an asteroid that formed approximately 650 million years ago. After travelling through space for millions of years, fragments of the iron meteorite fell in Australia’s Northern Territory approximately 4,200 years ago, creating a remarkable field of thirteen impact craters, the largest measuring up to approximately 130 metres across and 15 metres deep.

The crater field also holds considerable cultural significance for the local Arrernte people. Traditionally regarded as a sacred place, it is associated with the name ‘Chindu China Waru Chingi Yabu’, approximately translated as ‘Sun Walk Fire Devil Rock’. Although the craters were recorded by Europeans in 1899, their meteoritic origin was not scientifically established until 1931.

Founded in 1834, Charles Frodsham & Co. is the oldest continuously operating maker of precision chronometers. Renowned throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries for its marine chronometers, clocks and exceptional pocket watches, the firm played a pivotal role in the advancement of precision timekeeping. In the modern era, the focus is on the production of wristwatches, with no more than a dozen pieces being constructed annually.

The present Double Impulse Chronometer, delivered on 5 March 2024 and the third example ever produced in this particular configuration, is housed in an elegant 42.2 mm white gold case whose refined architecture reflects the technical originality of the movement within. Distinguished by its stepped bezel, alternating brushed and polished surfaces, and satin-finished caseband, the case also features an unusually positioned crown between 2 and 3 o'clock. This asymmetrical arrangement was adopted to preserve the ideal layout of the movement while maintaining a centrally positioned subsidiary seconds display. The exhibition caseback is secured by an eleven-sided bezel and bears traditional British hallmarks, including the crowned gold mark and the leopard's head of the Goldsmiths' Company of London, a hallmark that has certified precious metal objects since the fourteenth century.

At the heart of the watch lies one of the most remarkable mechanical achievements of contemporary independent watchmaking. Developed over sixteen years, the manually wound Frodsham movement incorporates George Daniels' Double Impulse Escapement, previously utilised by Daniels in seven large pocket chronometers including his two Space Traveller's watches, and by Derek Pratt in a tourbillon wristwatch. Beneath the imposing large diameter free-sprung balance, with a proprietary shock protection system, and supported by a graceful black-polished three-armed bridge, two independent escape wheels alternately engage a titanium detent, each powered by its own dedicated gear train and mainspring barrel. 

This unique architecture delivers exceptionally stable transmission of energy, enhancing chronometric precision. A sophisticated synchronisation mechanism, using a balance brake, ensures both barrels remain perfectly coordinated, explaining why the movement only begins running once fully wound, thereafter providing approximately 40 hours of power reserve. The discreet state of wind mechanism with differential sun and planet gearing, is read from the snail wheel mounted within the winding wheels. The engraved movement number continues the historic serial sequence inaugurated by John Arnold in 1761 and perpetuated by Charles Frodsham following the acquisition of Arnold's business in 1843, linking the present timepiece directly to one of the greatest traditions of English chronometer making.

The dial reflects the same uncompromising pursuit of precision and refinement. Crafted from zirconium oxide ceramic, it possesses the luminous appearance of grand feu enamel while offering superior long-term stability. The applied Arabic numerals and distinctive pointer-style hands are all heat-treated to a rich purple hue, providing exceptional contrast against the pristine white dial. Inspired by an early twentieth-century Frodsham Tourbillon watch, both hour and minute hands share the same length despite their differing visual weight, while the brand signature and minute and seconds tracks are applied by vapour deposition rather than conventional printing. The absence of the optional historical cyphers results in a particularly clean and contemporary aesthetic, perfectly complementing the extraordinary movement beneath.

Of these, just 41 were fitted with calibre 2891, comprising 12 watches in white gold, such as the present timepiece, and the remainder in platinum as reference 25945PT.

In watchmaking, a carillon employs three or more hammers to produce a richer and more melodious sequence of notes. In calibre 2891, three black-polished hammers strike three peripheral gongs to indicate the hours, quarters and minutes. The mechanism can be activated on demand through the pusher at 10 o’clock, while a three-position selector at 2 o’clock allows the wearer to choose between silence, grande sonnerie and petite sonnerie modes.

Developed by Renaud et Papi and first incorporated into a wristwatch calibre in 2000, the dynamograph indicates the real-time torque delivered by the mainspring through a direct barrel-force sensor. Particularly useful for an energy-intensive grande sonnerie, it allows the wearer to identify the optimal operating range of the mainspring and when additional winding is required.

Comprising an impressive 496 components, the manually wound calibre 2891 incorporates two superimposed barrels and a monometallic balance with lever escapement. The sonnerie provides approximately 60 hours of operation in petite sonnerie mode or 20 hours in grande sonnerie mode, while the going train offers approximately 48 hours of autonomy. Beautifully finished with Côtes de Genève, bevelled and polished edges and black-polished hammers, calibre 2891 combines one of watchmaking’s most prestigious traditional complications with remarkable mechanical innovation.

Dennison
Dennison's story began 175 years ago with Aaron Lufkin Dennison, regarded as the father of American watchmaking. His journey took him from America to Switzerland and then to Britain, where he established the Dennison Watch Case Company. Along the way, Dennison helped define modern watchmaking, registering patents and developing new metal alloys for cases. From co-founding Waltham in the U.S. to building one of the world’s largest case manufacturers in Britain, Dennison’s vision continues to inspire the ethos carried forward by the brand today.

For the best part of the 20th century, Dennison was renowned for designing and producing cases for brands such as Rolex, Omega, IWC, Jaeger-LeCoultre and Zenith, the very brands that shaped the industry as we know it today. For over 50 years, Dennison manufactured watch cases and other instruments for the British military. In that time, the company developed an undeniable reputation for excellence. It is no wonder, then, that no fewer than thirteen Smiths watches built with Dennison ‘Aquatite’ cases made the trip to the summit when Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first climbed Everest, or that a Dennison-cased watch was on the wrist of Lt. Commander Lithgow when he broke the world air-speed record flying the Supermarine Swift.

The historic Dennison watch brand was officially relaunched in late 2024, more than 50 years after the original British case-making company ceased operations in 1967. Now led by a team of passionate watch lovers, the Dennison back catalogue was explored for inspiration. A treasure trove of documents, images and timepieces was discovered, helping to steer the direction of the brand.

World-famous watch designer Emmanuel Gueit was chosen to bring the collection to life. Emmanuel, who has designed watches for Audemars Piguet, Rolex, Piaget and more, has created something indelible: a collection that picks up right where Dennison left off in the 1960s.

Created exclusively for the Watches for ELA charity auction, it represents the conclusion of a defining chapter in the history of the manufacture while supporting a cause dedicated to funding research and bringing hope to children and families affected by leukodystrophies.

- A unique watch.

For Felipe Pikullik, creating a unique watch for such a meaningful cause called for something deeply personal. The Mondphase I has always reflected one of his greatest passions: astronomy. At the same time, skeletonised watchmaking has been at the heart of his creative language since the earliest years of the atelier. Many of his first creations explored the beauty of exposing a movement's architecture, allowing the mechanics themselves to become part of the design.

For Watches for ELA, these two worlds come together for the first and only time. Rather than revisiting one of the existing executions, Felipe chose to reinterpret the Mondphase I through skeletonisation. The dial architecture has been opened completely, revealing the movement beneath and allowing the mechanics to become the face of the watch itself. Skeletonised black rhodium-plated brass bridges with hand-polished bevels create a striking dialogue between light and shadow, while the signature three-dimensional moon continues to float above the movement as the emotional centre of the composition.

With the introduction of the Mondphase II and the manufacture-developed FPMP2 calibre, the original Mondphase I reached the end of its journey. Some watches mark the beginning of a new chapter. Others bring one to its final conclusion. The Mondphase I belongs to the latter.

Originally introduced in two editions of twenty pieces each, the Mondphase I became the watch that established Felipe Pikullik's distinctive interpretation of astronomical watchmaking. One edition featured a black rhodium dial, while the second was crafted from genuine meteorite. Together, only forty examples were ever produced.

Approximately six additional hours of firing were necessary across the two components to fix and reveal the depth of the colours. In total, no fewer than 66 hours of artistic work and firing were devoted solely to these two miniature compositions.

The front and reverse of the 65’27” Tree of Life Unique Piece are therefore conceived as two chapters of the same narrative. Independent watchmaker Konstantin Chaykin’s celebrated Wristmons offer an imaginative and instantly recognisable interpretation of mechanical watchmaking. With the extraordinary ‘Seneca II’ pièce unique, Chaykin combines the playful character of the collection with a philosophical and philanthropic dimension, creating a one-of-a-kind timepiece specifically to benefit ELA.

The watch is dedicated to Lucius Annaeus Seneca the Younger, the celebrated Roman Stoic philosopher and moralist. Its conception draws inspiration from the phrase attributed to Seneca, ‘Non fructum beneficiorum sequi’: ‘Not to pursue the reward of good deeds’, a particularly fitting sentiment for a watch created for charitable purposes. The familiar Wristmon ‘face’ is formed by the hours at 10 o’clock and minutes at 2 o’clock, while Chaykin has introduced an additional complication: a date indication.

The date display is perhaps the most ingenious expression of the watch’s philosophical inspiration. Latin letters are incorporated into the date numerals so that, as the days progress throughout the month, they gradually spell out Seneca’s phrase ‘Non fructum beneficiorum sequi’. In this way, the charitable message is integrated directly into the mechanical and visual identity of the watch rather than serving merely as a decorative inscription.

The Seneca
The calendar indications themselves provide a further connection with ancient Rome. The Roman Republican calendar, traditionally associated with Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, was based upon the lunar month. Chaykin therefore chose to equip the Seneca with both a date display and a moon-phase indication. The latter forms the characteristic lunar ‘smile’ of the Wristmon, inverted from the conventional orientation and a defining feature of the collection since the introduction of the now-celebrated ‘Joker’ in 2017.

Chaykin frequently explores connections between philosophy, design and the history of timekeeping, and the Seneca develops this approach through its references to the evolution of the calendar in ancient Rome. The 12-month system familiar today emerged from Julius Caesar’s calendar reforms of 45 BC, while the seven-day week was subsequently adopted by the Romans. By drawing upon this historical context and the writings of Seneca, Chaykin has created a unique Wristmon in which the calendar, moon phases and distinctive anthropomorphic display combine to express both the passage of time and the philanthropic purpose for which the watch was conceived.

A Dial of Ice and Wood
The Iced Sea Unique Piece features a striking dial embedded with fragments of ancient wood, often millennia old, that have been preserved while trapped in glacial ice. To create this complexly layered dial, Montblanc's watchmakers first worked with mountaineers in France's Chamonix Valley to source subfossil wood from the Mer de Glace's moraine, a large layer of natural debris pushed against Mont Blanc's northern slope by the glacier. The sourced wood is then cut into shavings and arranged in a seemingly random, yet carefully distributed, array. The result is a natural-looking pattern of scattered subfossil wood. Next, a transparent resin is applied over the wood shavings, and a black colour is applied below, thus forming a sheet from which the dial is made. Finally, this resin surface is treated with a frozen finish that mimics the striated crystalline patterns of ice.

Glaciers in Motion
Over centuries, the slow movement of glaciers has carved some of Earth's most stunning geological features. As glaciers form and recede, they expose and relocate fertile soil. In the process, many felled trees become preserved as subfossils and are pushed into a glacier's moraine, the dense mass of sediment a glacier deposits at its outer edge. Montblanc pays homage to this special geological formation, also found in the Mer de Glace, the largest glacier on the Mont Blanc massif. Its geologically complex moraine, developed over time, has been captured in the dial of the timepiece with shavings of preserved trees found at the glacier.

The Earthy Tones of Distressed Steel
Finding inspiration in the elements, Montblanc presents a reimagined take on its Iced Sea Automatic Date Unique Piece, featuring a distressed steel finish. To achieve this, Montblanc has treated the stainless steel case and bracelet with a black coating, which is then distressed by washing and brushing with quartzite, a very hard mineral sourced from the Mont Blanc mountain itself. This process results in a blackened, distressed appearance that offers an organic aesthetic.

A Case for Adventure
The Montblanc Iced Sea Automatic Date 0 Oxygen Unique Piece features a 41 mm stainless steel case that allows the watch to withstand the demands of high-pressure underwater environments. The timepiece is water-resistant to 30 bar (approx. 300 metres), with subtle chamfering and elevated finishing along the gently curved lugs. Notably, the case is also fitted with Montblanc's 0 Oxygen technology. By removing oxygen from the case, the risk of condensation inside is mitigated, allowing enhanced performance in conditions where drastic fluctuations in atmospheric pressure and temperature are common.

Distressed Steel Bracelet

The enamel scene is entirely hand-painted and signed by Giancarlo Menni, one of the last great enamellists capable of perpetuating the supremely exacting art of miniature painting on enamel. Each unique creation could require anywhere from several months to as long as two years to complete. Working in Geneva during the late 20th century, Menni is believed to have painted approximately 50 miniature enamels for Patek Philippe, including interpretations of celebrated works and subjects such as Renoir’s Déjeuner des Canotiers in 1990, a Picasso clown in 1989 and Canaletto’s Canale Grande in 1984.

For centuries, fine enamelling has been used to decorate and enrich watches, jewelry and objets d’art. Patek Philippe has played an important role in maintaining the rare craft of miniature enamelling, traditionally associated with the finest Geneva timepieces and regarded as one of the most demanding of all the decorative arts. Such watches were generally created as unique pieces and often made to special order, with the subject selected by the client. Their miniature paintings could reproduce celebrated works of art, portraits and famous personalities, or even depict members of the future owner’s family.

The present timepiece is one of the highly sought-after early examples of F.P. Journe’s Chronomètre à Résonance, distinguished by its rhodium-plated brass movement. Introduced in 2000, these early watches belong to the formative period of François-Paul Journe’s eponymous manufacture, before he famously transitioned to movements crafted in 18k pink gold in 2004. Fewer than 400 brass-movement examples of the Chronomètre à Résonance are believed to have been produced, making them particularly coveted among collectors of early F.P. Journe.

The Chronomètre à Résonance was the result of years of experimentation and development before entering production. Like the Tourbillon Souverain, it was initially offered in 2000 through a ‘Souscription’ series of 20 watches, numbered 1 to 20. Through this subscription system, clients paid in advance, providing François-Paul Journe with the funds necessary to produce and deliver the watches. These earliest examples bear the suffix ‘00R’, indicating the year 2000 together with the letter ‘R’ for ‘Résonance’.

Following the Souscription series, the first production examples of reference ‘R’ were manufactured between 2000 and 2004. Housed in elegant 38 mm. cases available in platinum or 18k pink gold, they were offered with dials in white, pink or yellow gold. Among the most recognisable characteristics of these early brass-movement watches is the construction of the subsidiary dial frames, which are secured by distinctive bell-shaped screw lugs. This differs from the softer, more integrated design adopted on the later pink gold movement examples and provides a subtle visual distinction between the earliest and subsequent generations of the model.

The Chronomètre à Résonance
The Chronomètre à Résonance remains one of François-Paul Journe’s most ingenious and important creations. Its fundamental principle can be traced to Christiaan Huygens, who observed in 1665 that two pendulum clocks suspended from the same support would eventually synchronise their oscillations. The phenomenon subsequently fascinated some of history’s greatest watchmakers, notably Antide Janvier and Abraham-Louis Breguet, the latter applying the principle to a small number of exceptional resonance pocket watches during the early 19th century.

François-Paul Journe succeeded in adapting this centuries-old phenomenon to the wristwatch. The Chronomètre à Résonance employs two independent regulating systems positioned in close proximity, allowing their balances to influence one another through resonance and synchronise their rates. Once in resonance, the two oscillators work in harmony, helping to compensate for disturbances encountered during everyday wear.

By successfully translating this fascinating physical phenomenon into a wristwatch, François-Paul Journe created one of the defining complications of contemporary independent watchmaking. Combining an intellectually compelling mechanical principle with the distinctive aesthetic and technical language of his earliest production, the brass-movement Chronomètre à Résonance occupies a particularly important position in the history of the manufacture.

Presented in June 2022, the Zenith x Kari Voutilainen Calibre 135-O represents one of the most extraordinary collaborations in modern watchmaking. During a review of its archives, Zenith rediscovered a small number of calibre 135-O movements, the legendary observatory chronometer calibres that had competed in the prestigious Neuchâtel Observatory trials between 1950 and 1954. The suffix 'O' denotes Observatoire, reflecting their exclusive purpose as competition movements rather than commercial products. Conceived specifically for chronometry contests, the calibre was designed around a 30 mm diameter, the maximum permitted for the wristwatch category, and a large 14 mm balance wheel, paired with an oversized barrel to maximise precision, stability, and consistent power delivery.

Manufactured between 1949 and 1962, the calibre 135 existed in two distinct forms: the commercial calibre 135 and the exceptionally rare calibre 135-O, reserved exclusively for observatory competitions. Never intended for sale, the 135-O achieved an unrivalled record of more than 230 chronometry awards, making it the most decorated competition movement in the history of watchmaking. Fitted with Guillaume balances and meticulously regulated by Zenith's celebrated chronométriers, Charles Fleck and René Gygax, the present movement was adjusted by the latter before competing at the 1954 Neuchâtel Observatory trials, where it achieved a First Prize distinction.

Because these movements were built solely as precision instruments, their finishing prioritised performance over aesthetics and they were never intended to be cased as wristwatches. After remaining dormant for more than six decades, each movement underwent an exhaustive restoration under the direction of master watchmaker Kari Voutilainen. Between 2020 and 2022, Voutilainen and his team completely dismantled every calibre, inspected each individual component, restored the original tolerances, and reassembled the movement before applying the exceptional hand-finishing for which the Finnish master is internationally renowned. The result is a remarkable union of one of the greatest chronometry movements ever created with one of contemporary independent watchmaking's finest finishing ateliers.

The present timepiece is further accompanied by a remarkable presentation box inspired by the original wooden storage cases in which these observatory movements had been preserved for decades. Constructed from two wooden halves secured by brass fittings, it pays homage to the movement's extraordinary provenance. Even more significantly, the original historical movement box is supplied alongside the watch, providing an exceptional link to its competition history.

Just eleven calibre 135-O movements were selected for this remarkable project. Of these, only ten were cased in platinum with a black dial, while the eleventh was reserved for a unique charity piece, making the present timepiece one of the rarest and most historically significant contemporary collaborations ever undertaken by Zenith.

F.P. Journe Dual Time-Zone
Local time at the wearer’s current location is indicated by the blued steel hands, which are linked to the calendar to display the corresponding geographical date and time. A gilt steel hand indicates home time against the 24-hour chapter ring, itself linked to the 24 time zones represented on the painted globe.

Local time is adjusted by pulling the three-position crown to its third position. To set the second time zone, the crown is pulled to its second position and turned clockwise, while turning it anticlockwise adjusts the date. The globe is adjusted using the secured pusher in the caseband at 4 o’clock, positioning the home time zone at 0 for winter time. The gold hand simultaneously adjusts to the corresponding hour in that time zone. The +1 / -1 indications allow the wearer to account for summer time according to whether the geographical location lies east or west of the selected zone.

Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)
Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) originally referred to solar time observed at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London. Adopted as the official time standard throughout Great Britain in 1880, it subsequently became the principal international time standard for much of the 20th century.

In 1972, GMT was superseded as the international civil time standard by Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Whereas GMT is historically based on the Earth’s rotation and mean solar time, UTC is derived from International Atomic Time, calculated using the combined measurements of hundreds of highly precise atomic clocks around the world. This atomic basis provides the exceptionally stable international reference upon which modern civil timekeeping is founded.

The Rudis Sylva Harmonious Oscillator RS12 stands as one of the most original creations of contemporary independent watchmaking. Presented by the Jura-based manufacture Rudis Sylva, the model combines exceptional traditional craftsmanship with a genuinely innovative regulating system: the patented Harmonious Oscillator. Conceived around two mechanically coupled balance wheels linked by a differential, the RS12 explores an entirely different approach to improving chronometric stability while offering one of the most captivating visual displays in modern horology.

Unlike resonance systems based on the physical transmission of vibrations through the movement, such as that developed by François-Paul Journe, the Harmonious Oscillator relies on direct mechanical interaction. The Dials of Nautilus reference 3700⁄1
Created by Stern Frères, the distinctive striped dials of the Nautilus were entirely hand-made – each line recess is engraved separately. To achieve the aptly named 'gray depth of ocean' colour specified by Patek Philippe the dials were painted alternately black and blue several times and then covered with a protective 'Zapon' varnish. Early examples often display a degradation of the varnish so that depending on how a watch has been stored over the years, an individual dial may have tropicalized more towards either blue, gray, chestnut or green.

The indexes and hands are made of gold (sometimes erroneously called “steel” on some Extracts from the archives) and filled with luminescent material. The Patek Philippe signature and the outer minute divisions were painted. Below the 6 o’clock index is the word “Swiss” flanked on each side by the 'Aprior' mark of two sigma symbols. The Aprior mark was conferred by the 'Association pour la Promotion Industrielle de l’Or' on dials made of solid gold or at least with solid gold indexes.

The Nautilus Waterproof Case Ref. 3700⁄1
The patent for the case design of the original Nautilus reference 3700⁄1 was registered on 23 April 1976. The cases were made for Patek Philippe by Favre-Perret SA, from 1976 until 1981, when production was transferred to Patek’s own Ateliers Réunis workshops. It comprises two parts, the main body and the bezel, at each side is an 'ear' which couples with a corresponding flange, the two parts are secured by lateral screws. A rubber seal sits between the bezel and case body and is thus compressed when subject to water pressure forming a perfect watertight seal. Extremely rare and produced in very small numbers, Universal Genève cloisonné enamel wristwatches have become highly sought-after rarities among discerning collectors. The present example is particularly distinguished by its magnificent polychrome cloisonné enamel dial depicting Saint George on horseback. The composition is complemented by Arabic numerals and triangular hour markers, which enhance both its legibility and visual appeal without detracting from the intricate enamel decoration. Housed in an elegant 18k pink gold case with gracefully downturned lugs and powered by a manually wound Universal Genève movement, the watch combines exceptional decorative artistry with the refined proportions and understated elegance characteristic of fine mid-century watchmaking.

Enamelling is among the most complex and demanding decorative arts in watchmaking, and the present timepiece represents a particularly fine example of the celebrated cloisonné technique. The process begins with the meticulous application of delicate gold wires to the dial, creating individual compartments known as cloisons, which define the outlines of the composition. Each compartment is then carefully filled with finely ground enamel powder in precisely selected colours before the dial is fired at high temperatures, allowing the enamel to fuse and settle. To achieve the desired depth, richness of colour and flawless finish, this painstaking procedure must be repeated numerous times, with each successive firing presenting the risk of cracking or distortion caused by thermal stress.

Adding further complexity to the process, the colours of the enamel undergo subtle transformations during firing, requiring the master enameller to anticipate the final result with extraordinary precision and expertise. Consequently, polychrome cloisonné enamelling remains an exceptionally demanding and costly decorative technique, mastered by only a small number of highly skilled artisans. The extraordinary rarity of these dials, combined with their remarkable artistic execution and captivating visual presence, places watches such as the present example among the most desirable and visually striking vintage wristwatches available to collectors today.

The Cartier Tank needs almost no introduction. Undoubtedly one of the most recognisable and desirable wristwatches in the world, its simplicity, beauty and elegance have transcended the passing fashions of successive decades. Indeed, the timeless appeal of the Cartier Tank brings to mind the words of the great Yves Saint Laurent: ‘Fashions fade, style is eternal’. Naturally, numerous variations of the classic Tank have been created since its introduction in 1918. Among the rarest and most seldom seen is the platinum-cased Tank Louis Cartier.

The present superb example, dating from the 1960s, was made during a period when Cartier Paris produced wristwatches in extremely small quantities. Housed in a solid platinum case, it bears traditional French platinum hallmarks, hand-stamped serial numbers and the distinctive punch mark of Edmond Jaeger, comprising the initials ‘EJ’ within a lozenge. Possessing an extraordinarily chic and understated elegance, the timepiece is further distinguished by its probably original, numbered platinum deployant clasp, likewise bearing the Edmond Jaeger punch mark.

The classic Tank Louis Cartier enjoys considerable cachet and remains one of the most eagerly sought-after models among collectors today. Vintage platinum examples are particularly elusive, appearing only exceptionally rarely on the market. To the best of our knowledge, the present timepiece is one of only a very small handful of vintage platinum Tank Louis Cartier examples ever to have been offered at international auction, further underlining its extraordinary rarity and desirability.

Few wristwatches have had as profound an impact on modern watchmaking as Audemars Piguet's Royal Oak. Introduced in 1972, it revolutionised the industry by becoming the first serially produced stainless steel wristwatch positioned as a true luxury timepiece, a concept considered remarkably unconventional at the time. Designed by the legendary Gérald Genta, whose creations would go on to shape the identities of some of the world's greatest watch manufactures, the Royal Oak has since become one of the most recognisable and influential wristwatch designs ever produced. Its distinctive octagonal bezel, secured by eight hexagonal screws, was famously inspired by the portholes of traditional diving helmets.

Introduced in 2012, reference 15450ST continued the legacy of reference 15300 as the elegant mid-sized interpretation of the Royal Oak. Measuring 37 mm., it faithfully preserves the model's iconic design language, combining the beautifully finished stainless steel case and integrated bracelet with the signature blue 'Grande Tapisserie' dial. At its heart beats the in-house calibre 3120, offering a power reserve of approximately 60 hours and renowned for its robustness and refined finishing. Now discontinued and succeeded by the reference 15550ST, the 15450ST has become an increasingly sought-after reference among collectors who appreciate its balanced proportions and timeless versatility.

During the 1980s, celebrated watch designer Gérald Genta secured the licence to create wristwatches featuring Walt Disney's beloved characters, transforming some of the world's most recognisable animated figures into sophisticated examples of watchmaking. These creations combined playful artistry with mechanically inventive complications, quickly becoming some of the most distinctive and sought-after models in Genta's extraordinary work.

The present Gérald Genta Retro Fantasy, housed in a generous 36 mm case, is among the largest executions of the celebrated collection. It features one of the rarer Disney scenes, depicting Mickey Mouse playing golf. In characteristic Gérald Genta fashion, the animation is seamlessly integrated into the time display: Mickey's golf club serves as the retrograde minute hand, while the jumping hour is displayed through the aperture at 4 o'clock, creating an engaging and highly original way of telling the time.

The finely detailed Mickey Mouse figure is beautifully contrasted against a luminous mother-of-pearl dial, whose iridescent silver-blue and delicate pink reflections continually change with the light. Further enhancing its luxurious appearance, the bezel is lavishly set with a double row of diamonds, beautifully framing the playful dial while emphasizing the watch's jewel-like character.

https://www.christies.com/en/lot/lot-661.catalogue_note:
Gérald Genta is universally regarded as one of the most influential watch designers in history. Responsible for shaping some of the most iconic wristwatches ever created, including landmark designs for Audemars Piguet, Patek Philippe, Cartier, and numerous other prestigious manufactures, he transformed the language of modern watchmaking through his bold creativity and visionary approach. Under his own name, however, Genta enjoyed complete artistic freedom, allowing him to explore some of the most mechanically ambitious creations of the late twentieth century. His celebrated 'Grande Sonnerie' held the distinction of being the world's most complicated serially produced wristwatch for several years during the 1990s, while his independent creations have increasingly come to be recognised as milestones of contemporary high watchmaking.

The present timepiece showcases one of Gérald Genta's most unusual and captivating complications: the retrograde hours display. Rather than completing a conventional circular rotation, the hour hand travels along a semi-circular scale before instantaneously returning to its starting position. This ingenious arrangement leaves the centre of the dial unobstructed, providing a spectacular view of the magnificent one-minute tourbillon. The tourbillon carriage itself doubles as the running seconds indication, distinguished by its characteristic red seconds hand, creating a constantly animated display that perfectly balances mechanical ingenuity with visual spectacle.

Further enhancing the extraordinary character of the watch, the case is lavishly adorned with a double row of diamonds. According to the accompanying Certificate of Origin, a total of 102 diamonds weighing approximately 2.93 carats embellish the case, introducing an exceptional jewellery dimension to Genta's already unconventional design.

The refined design is further enhanced by a diamond-set winding crown and a matching pink gold ardillon buckle, also set with diamonds, creating a harmonious continuity throughout the timepiece.
